summary: Chris Koerner and Nick compare how entrepreneurs use AI tools and discuss lessons from 30 interviews. They describe ChatGPT as a thought partner, Claude as a coding partner, Perplexity for research, and Gemini for Google Workspace workflows, while also discussing Cursor and Replit. The business opportunities raised include AI-assisted mediation, a certification and rating service, an AI model selection quiz, and AI sales workflows. A recurring takeaway is to focus AI on sales and other work that can be tied directly to revenue.

ideas.name: AI-assisted business mediation
ideas.one_liner: Use a ChatGPT wrapper or prompting system to help a mediator gather and process dispute information faster.
ideas.business_model: Mediation service billed for the mediator's time; the transcript suggests AI could increase capacity but does not state a software business model.
ideas.customer: Businesses and parties using a mediator to resolve disputes.
ideas.problem: A mediator's available time limits how many clients the business can serve.
ideas.offer: A mediation service using a ChatGPT wrapper or prompting system to collect and process information more quickly before mediation.

pricing.model: Mediation billing; exact pricing not stated.
pricing.notes: The transcript says the business can only bill for the work the mediator can personally do.

ideas.delivery: A human mediator handles the mediation. A ChatGPT-based wrapper or prompt system could help gather and organize the parties' information beforehand.
unit_economics_claims: The speaker speculates that saving an hour per mediation could let a mediator take on 20 more clients per month.

acquisition.how: No customer acquisition process is described; the mediation business itself would still need to find clients.

onboarding.how: A prompt system could collect information, but the parties would need to provide and review their accounts.

delivery.how: The mediator still conducts the mediation; AI is described as a way to prepare information faster.

billing.how: Billing could use software, but no automated billing process is described.

support.how: Dispute participants would still need access to a human mediator.

uk_applicability.notes: The workflow could apply in the UK, but mediation practice and dispute procedures may differ. Sensitive dispute information also needs careful handling.

risks: The parties would need to agree on what information is submitted and how the prompt is framed.
AI output may reflect an incomplete or one-sided account; the transcript notes that each person can provide biased context.
The AI system would assist a mediator rather than replace the human mediation process.

ideas.name: AI sales workflow automation
ideas.one_liner: Use AI for sales follow-up, lead tracking, after-hours calls, customer chat, and sales-call preparation.
ideas.business_model: No external vendor business model is stated; entrepreneurs describe using AI in their own sales operations.
ideas.customer: Businesses with sales teams or customer inquiries.
ideas.problem: Sales teams need to follow up with prospects, track leads, respond to customers, and prepare for calls.
ideas.offer: AI-assisted lead follow-up, lead tracking, after-hours phone service, customer chatbots, and preparation for sales calls.
ideas.delivery: The transcript describes AI being used by businesses for sales tasks, but does not explain a specific vendor, setup, or delivery process.

acquisition.how: No acquisition process is described; an implementation business would still need to reach prospective clients.

onboarding.how: Connecting a system to a business's leads and sales process would likely need setup and human checks.

delivery.how: AI can perform routine follow-ups and responses, while people would need to review exceptions and sales conversations.

billing.how: If offered as software or a managed service, recurring billing could be automated; no billing method is stated.

support.how: Customers may need human help with integrations, errors, and sales interactions that need judgment.

uk_applicability.notes: The sales workflows can apply in the UK, but automated marketing must follow UK PECR rules: unsolicited messages to individuals and sole traders generally need consent; cold email to limited companies is allowed, and cold calls must screen TPS/CTPS.

risks: Automated follow-up and customer messaging could breach UK PECR rules if sent without the required consent.
Poorly reviewed AI responses could mislead prospects or damage customer relationships.
The transcript reports these as use cases, not as a proven external AI automation business.

tactics.name: Test billboard slogans with geo-targeted social ads
steps: Use AI to generate candidate billboard slogans, keeping them short enough to read quickly.
Keep the podcast artwork and other ad copy the same so the slogan is the variable being tested.
Target people in the counties around the planned billboard and exclude people who have already interacted with the podcast.
Run the creative across Meta placements and compare cost per click.
Use the lowest-cost slogan as the billboard candidate.

quote.text: And then I just look at the clicks. Lowest cost per click wins. And then I get because it's 950 bucks to print that billboard.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Track billboard impact with a local download baseline
steps: Export podcast downloads by city from Buzzsprout before the billboard goes live.
Define the nearby cities to include and calculate their share of all-time downloads as a baseline.
Repeat the export weekly and compare the local share over time.
Interpret the result cautiously because the data counts downloads, not unique listeners, and other episodes can affect totals.

quote.text: I'm just going to run that export every week and see the raw number and the percentage as a ratio and see if it's climbing or not.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Compare AI predictions with paid ad results
steps: Give the same billboard slogans to several AI models and ask them to rank which will be most effective.
Run a real-world ad test with consistent creative and targeting.
Compare the model rankings with the actual click results to assess whether AI can shorten future testing.

quote.text: Rank these from what you think would be most to least effective. See what the four models spit out and then compare it to the actual results from Facebook ads.
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Aggregate interview transcripts into a searchable dataset
steps: Keep speaker names in the transcript data so findings can be analyzed by person.
Clean timestamps and dead space, then combine the transcripts in Google Colab.
Ask ChatGPT to create a Python script, then use Claude to debug it when it fails.
Connect the OpenAI API directly to the notebook if a Zapier connection is unnecessary.
Ask ChatGPT to format the resulting spreadsheet and summarize interviews.

quote.text: First couple times it doesn't work. Then I go to Claude. Claude fixes my Python script and it starts working.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use structured prompts to get more critical AI feedback
steps: Set a custom GPT role such as a hard-nosed content specialist.
Explain why direct, accurate feedback matters and ask for actionable critique.
Provide enough relevant context, then check whether the response reflects the information supplied.

quote.text: I have a custom GPT where in the GPT prompt, I'm like, you're a hard-nosed, nononsense content specialist. I need you to give me direct advice
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Ask AI to rank creative options, then iterate
steps: Ask an AI model to generate and rank candidate titles or slogans.
Iterate on promising candidates rather than accepting the first output.
For campaigns, test the candidates with real audiences and compare the results with the AI ranking.

quote.text: generate me the 10 best titles and rank them. And then I'll like iterate from there.

warnings.warning: AI can give overly flattering feedback or reflect the incentive to keep users engaged; the speakers advise not treating it as automatically unbiased.
If a user supplies one-sided or incomplete context, AI may return a one-sided answer. A shared mediation prompt would still require agreement on both the prompt and the output.

quote.text: if you feed it biased info, it's going to give you biased info.
quote.speaker: Nick

warnings.warning: Using AI to frame arguments in a relationship can create an unfair interaction if one person secretly uses the advice to persuade the other.

warnings.warning: Podcast download counts do not reveal the number of unique listeners, so a local increase may not mean a similar increase in new people.
A local download increase may have other causes, such as a popular episode; compare the local share with overall trends and treat attribution as imperfect.
An AI-generated app or workflow may be easy to start but difficult to finish; speakers describe incomplete Replit projects and note that some coding tools require coding experience.
UK outbound sales automation must follow PECR rules for electronic marketing and screen cold calls against TPS/CTPS.

lessons.lesson: Build products close to revenue: customers can more easily value tools that help them generate sales and tie the tool to money earned.

quote.text: build something that people can use to directly make more money and they know that your thing helped them generate more money
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

evidence_quality.rationale: Chris describes his own transcript-processing workflow and billboard test with concrete steps, and reports findings from interviews with 30 entrepreneurs. Most claims are not independently verified, several tool comparisons are based on interview impressions, and some business opportunities are speculative.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host promotes the Koerner Office podcast and free newsletter at tkopod.com. No paid sponsor or product sale is identified in the transcript.
